Moreton Bay trawler dolphins

eastern Moreton Bay, Queensland, Australia
trawler foraging
Foraging

"Trawlers provide a reliable food source for dolphins through the provision of usually unobtainable prey while trawler gear is in use and discarded by-catch. We refer to this as `trawler foraging’. Through the sounds of trawlers’ engines, food patches created by trawlers are detectable by dolphins...

Recorded from 1997 to 1999
Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Unknown
Evidence and details

Description: "Trawlers provide a reliable food source for dolphins through the provision of usually unobtainable prey while trawler gear is in use and discarded by-catch. We refer to this as `trawler foraging’. Through the sounds of trawlers’ engines, food patches created by trawlers are detectable by dolphins over kilometres" (Chilvers & Corkeron 2001)

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: "observations of a (probable) alliance of non-trawler males associated with trawler females suggest that genetic interchange between the two communities could occur. More importantly in the context of this paper, these observations also clearly demonstrate that members of the two communities can interact. Association analyses show that members of the two communities do not interact in other circumstances. As it is highly improbable that this non-interaction occurs by chance, it appears that the members of the two communities usually ignore each other. However, as we have no data on the dolphins’ social structure prior to the start of the trawl fishery in the1950s, we cannot demonstrate that trawling has caused the existing social structure. It is possible (to give one scenario) that the two communities existed separately prior to the trawl fishery and that the extent of overlap of their ranges is a result of changes in the ranging behaviour of what are now trawler dolphins" (Chilvers et al. 2001)

Oblique: suspected unknown

Domains: foraging

Anthropogenic effects: "the habitat usage patterns of members of the non-trawler community indicate that they rely heavily on sea grass areas for forging (Chilvers 2001). The effects of pollutants from urban run-off may threaten sea grass viability (e.g. Abal et al.1998; Prange & Dennison 2000) and recurrent blooms of the cyanobacterium Lyngbya majuscula are currently threatening sea grass beds in the non-trawler community’s range (see Collier 2000). The feeding opportunities for trawler dolphins that are created by trawling have become part of their habitat requirements, although trawler dolphins are capable of foraging on other food sources (e.g. at weekends when trawling is banned)" (Chilvers & Corkeron 2001)

Shark Bay dolphins

Eastern Gulf of Shark Bay, Western Australia 113°45′E, 25°48′S
sponging
Foraging

Sponging refers to covering the rostrum with a broken-off piece of marine sponge while searching for fishes in substrate.

Recorded from 1988 to 2002
Vertical: YesHorizontal: NoOblique: No
Evidence and details

Description: Sponging refers to covering the rostrum with a broken-off piece of marine sponge while searching for fishes in substrate. "At least four nonsponging females regularly forage in at least one of these channels without using a sponge (14), strongly indicating that both spongers and nonspongers use the same habitat for foraging. Males also are regularly seen foraging in all sponging channels (R.C.C., unpublished data), ruling out the possibility that the occurrence of sponging is due to ecological differences alone...Between 2001 and 2004, 45 of the 65 adult males whose home ranges overlap with the sponging area consorted 11 sponge carriers in 34 documented consortships. Males engaging in this behavior account for at least 88.2% of all paternities that were assigned in a previous study (13). Only 2 (2.2%) of all 90 consortship places were occupied by the single known adult male sponge carrier, suggesting that almost all offspring of spongers are sired by nonsponging males." (Krutzen et al. 2005)

Vertical: sponging affects echolocation- combination of difficulty and time needed to learn sponging and need to adapt to changes in reception of echolocation signals may be why the behavior is only transmitted vertically (Jacobs et al. 2025)

Horizontal: "Using mitochondrial DNA analyses, we show that sponging shows an almost exclusive vertical social transmission within a single matriline from mother to female offspring."

Oblique: "Using mitochondrial DNA analyses, we show that sponging shows an almost exclusive vertical social transmission within a single matriline from mother to female offspring."

prey inspection
Foraging

Dolphin calves in Shark Bay inspect prey caught by unrelated older dolphins:

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Yes
Evidence and details

Description: Dolphin calves in Shark Bay inspect prey caught by unrelated older dolphins: "Fish inspections then, defined as remaining <2 m to a dolphin that has a fish in its mouth, are unlikely to be “requests” for food. The inspections are obvious and distinct from typical social groupings in that dolphins are typically dispersed during foraging (e.g., Mann and Watson-Capps 2005), but following the fish catch, one or more dolphins rapidly (<0.5 min) approaches the dolphin that caught the fish. If the one that caught the fish continues swimming, then the inspectors stay very close (typically <1 m), with their head(s) near the prey item. Inspectors do not adopt echelon or calf position typical of calves (Mann and Smuts 1999), but are clearly oriented to the fish itself. If the fish owner remains stationary (hanging at the surface) with the fish in its mouth, then inspectors commonly form a star or semi-star formation around the fish, with their heads close to the fish. If the fish owner begins to break up the fish, the inspectors keep circling and diving down near the prey, but again, do not touch pieces that are floating close to their rostra." (Mann et al. 2007)

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: suspected unknown

Oblique: "Although calves are exposed to maternal foraging most frequently and to foraging by non-mothers infrequently, they clearly show an interest in prey caught by non-mothers. Thus, although vertical transmission appears to be the dominant influence on calf foraging development (e.g., Mann and Sargeant 2003), calves have opportunities for oblique social learning." (Mann et al. 2007)

Useless Loop dolphins

Useless Loop, Western Gulf of Shark Bay, Australia
shelling
Foraging

Dolphins lift conch shells and feed on prey trapped inside. “Dolphins utilize the shell to first entrap the prey before exposing it to gravity by lifting the shell above the water surface and shaking it about in order to dislodge the prey [17], thereby fulfilling these conditions and qualifying...

Vertical: Inferred noHorizontal: Inferred yesOblique: Inferred yes
Evidence and details

Description: Dolphins lift conch shells and feed on prey trapped inside. “Dolphins utilize the shell to first entrap the prey before exposing it to gravity by lifting the shell above the water surface and shaking it about in order to dislodge the prey [17], thereby fulfilling these conditions and qualifying shelling as tool use.” Unlike sponging, not female-biased. (Wild et al. 2020)

Vertical: Network-based diffusion analysis controlling for environmental and genetic factors supports non-vertical (horizontal and/or oblique) transmission of shelling behavior between associates. Best model indicates about 43% of dolphins may learn shelling asocially (Wild et al. 2020)

Horizontal: Network-based diffusion analysis controlling for environmental and genetic factors supports non-vertical (horizontal and/or oblique) transmission of shelling behavior between associates. Best model indicates about 43% of dolphins may learn shelling asocially (Wild et al. 2020)

Oblique: Network-based diffusion analysis controlling for environmental and genetic factors supports non-vertical (horizontal and/or oblique) transmission of shelling behavior between associates. Best model indicates about 43% of dolphins may learn shelling asocially (Wild et al. 2020)
